nameStory: The Stonewall Rim Lichen gets its name from its love of growing on the old stone walls that crisscross New England's landscape. The 'rim' part refers to the distinctive raised edges around its disc-like fruiting bodies, which look like tiny saucers with perfectly formed rims.
description: Stonewall Rim Lichen is a crusty, waxy-looking lichen that forms pale yellowish-green patches on rocks and stone walls. It typically grows in neat rosettes that radiate outward from a central point, like a botanical pinwheel. The patches are filled with small, disc-like fruiting bodies that have a yellowish-tan color and distinctive raised rims. Individual colonies can spread several inches across over many years.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms distinctive rosettes that radiate outward from a center point like spokes on a wheel, creating neat circular or semicircular patches on rock surfaces

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Overall pale yellowish-green with a waxy appearance that becomes more vibrant when wet, contrasting with the yellowish-tan fruiting discs

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Small disc-like fruiting bodies (apothecia) with raised rims that feel slightly elevated when you run your finger across them - like tiny saucers embedded in the lichen

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Waxy, smooth surface that feels slightly slippery when wet and appears crusty when dry, firmly attached to the rock substrate

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found growing on rocks, stone walls, concrete, and other hard mineral surfaces - rarely on wood or soil

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual rosettes typically 1-4 inches across, but can merge with neighboring colonies to cover larger areas of rock surface

habitat: Look for Stonewall Rim Lichen on the countless stone walls, rock outcrops, and granite boulders scattered throughout New England's forests and fields. It thrives on both natural rock faces and human-made stone structures like old foundations and cemetery headstones. This lichen prefers sunny to partially shaded locations and is common from sea level up into the mountains.

seasonality.spring: Colors become more vibrant with spring rains, showing bright yellowish-green tones. New growth begins as temperatures warm and moisture increases.
seasonality.summer: May appear duller and more grayish during dry periods, but the distinctive rosette pattern and rimmed fruiting bodies remain clearly visible.
seasonality.fall: Often looks its best in fall with moderate moisture and cooler temperatures bringing out the waxy, pale green coloration.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible under snow and continues slow growth. Colors may appear more muted but the raised fruiting body rims create shadows that make identification easier.

funFact: This lichen is so cosmopolitan that it grows on every continent except Antarctica - the same species you find on a New England stone wall also thrives on ancient ruins in Europe and rocky outcrops in Asia, making it one of the most widely distributed lichens on Earth.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other yellowish rock lichens, but the neat rosette growth pattern radiating from a center is distinctive - other similar lichens tend to grow in irregular patches without the spoke-like arrangement.
contextualKnowledge: Scientists debate whether this is actually one highly variable species or a complex of several closely related species that look nearly identical - the 'species' you're looking at might actually be several different ones that we haven't figured out how to tell apart yet.
compareHints: Since this is the only member of its genus in New England, compare it to other common rock lichens in the same family. It's paler and greener than the honey-colored rock lichens, and more yellow than the gray-green species. The rosette growth pattern and rimmed fruiting bodies are key distinguishing features from its relatives.
